sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities fell as a sharp AI-related technology sell-off, a hotter-than-expected US inflation print and the start of Q3 earnings season drove a rotation out of mega-cap growth into value and defensives. MSCI World slipped roughly **1%** to about **4,908** (approx., verify before merging), with MSCI Developed Markets similar and MSCI Emerging Markets down around **2%** near **1,660** (approx., verify before merging). In the US the S&P 500 fell **1.9%** to **7,659.44**, while the MAG7 mega-cap cohort tumbled about **5.4%** (approx., verify before merging), led lower by chip names. Europe bucked the trend, with the Euro Stoxx 50 up around **0.6%** to **6,204**. In APAC, Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped roughly **5.4%** to **65,324** (approx., verify before merging) despite a Friday bounce, Hong Kong's Hang Seng ended near **24,187** and China's CSI 300 was broadly flat at **4,171**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities fell sharply as a sell-off in AI-linked technology, a hotter-than-expected September inflation print and the opening of Q3 earnings season pushed investors from large-cap growth towards value and defensives. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slumped **4.48%** to **26,140.03** — its worst week since June — and the S&P 500 fell **1.9%** to **7,659.44**, while the Dow bucked the trend, adding **0.67%** to **52,002.41** on defensive rotation.

The MAG7 cohort shed roughly **5.4%**, with Nvidia down about **5.8%** as semiconductors logged their longest losing streak since 2006 amid fears over AI financing conditions, tied to neocloud debt and Chinese memory competition. Hotter CPI, with headline inflation near **3.7%** y/y, revived worries about further Fed tightening and a higher cost of capital.

Leadership shifted decisively, with the equal-weighted S&P 500 posting its best week versus the cap-weighted tech cohort since 2009. Defensive and value sectors held up as rate-sensitive growth, communications and small caps — the Russell 2000 fell **3.05%** — bore the brunt of the de-risking.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities outperformed, advancing as the rotation away from richly valued US technology favoured the region's more value-heavy indices. The pan-regional STOXX Europe 600 rose roughly **1.4%** to around **645**, while the Euro Stoxx 50 added about **0.6%** to **6,204** and Germany's DAX closed near **25,623**.

The gains came despite sticky inflation, with euro-area CPI accelerating to **3.8%** in September, keeping the ECB cautious on the policy path. France's CAC 40 climbed around **1.7%**, whereas the UK's FTSE 100 lagged the region, slipping late in the week.

Dispersion was notable: value-oriented financials, industrials and defensives underpinned the regional advance, while globally exposed technology names tracked the US sell-off lower. Steadier eurozone bond yields and relative valuation appeal supported demand into Friday's close.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equities fell over the week, led lower by Japan, where the Nikkei 225 dropped roughly **5.4%** to **65,324.29** — its steepest weekly decline since July — as the global AI and semiconductor sell-off hit chip-related names hard, though the index rebounded **1.39%** on Friday.

Chinese markets proved more resilient: the CSI 300 ended broadly flat at **4,170.61** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng steadied near **24,186.83**, rising **0.52%** on Friday as chipmakers recovered part of their losses. South Korea's Kospi rallied **2.05%** to **5,668.05** into the close.

The regional tone was dominated by the AI-valuation debate, with concerns over Chinese semiconductor competition, AI infrastructure returns and financing conditions weighing on higher-beta tech. A broad Friday bounce across the region pared weekly losses as sentiment stabilised alongside firmer US futures.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar stayed firm, with Convera's latest report ('Reality bytes') noting the index consolidating just above the **102** level. The greenback touched an 18-month high of **102.945** on Wednesday after the hotter September inflation print, before paring gains as the equity sell-off sparked a bond rally and tempered Fed-hike pricing.

The euro was rangebound, with EUR/USD hovering around **1.12**; Convera judged much of the French fiscal pessimism as priced in but saw limited scope for a sustained recovery. Sterling was comparatively steady, while the yen stayed soft against the firm dollar as wide rate differentials persisted.

Risk-off flows late in the week offered the yen and other haven currencies modest support, whereas higher-beta emerging-market currencies came under pressure from the equity slide and elevated US yields, reinforcing the dollar's broad resilience.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities were a split market, with Saxo noting gold steadying while oil tightness and growth fears divided the complex; the Bloomberg Commodity Index finished roughly flat on the week.

Gold held firm, supported by falling real yields amid the equity sell-off and robust investment demand, with ETF holdings reaching a four-year high. Crude remained underpinned by physical tightness — elevated refinery margins, firm freight costs and tight distillate markets — even as broader growth concerns capped the upside.

Industrial metals diverged: copper outperformed, buoyed by electrification and data-centre demand, though speculators trimmed net length by about **22%** to a three-month low. Iron ore weakened on China's construction slump, underscoring the uneven demand backdrop across the sector.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign bonds whipsawed. The hotter September inflation data initially drove yields higher on revived tightening fears, before a mid-week equity sell-off sparked a safe-haven bond rally that pulled them back. The 10-year UST ended near **5.08%** and the 2-year around **4.73%**, each easing roughly **1bp** on Friday.

Rate expectations stayed hawkish by recent standards: markets priced a roughly **87%** chance the Fed holds this month after September's unanimous vote to lift rates to **3.75–4%**, with October hike odds below **20%**. Comments from Fed Chair Warsh and sticky inflation kept the higher-for-longer narrative firmly in play.

Credit tone softened with the equity de-risking, as weakness in technology and communications weighed on risk appetite; HY spreads came under modest pressure while IG proved comparatively resilient, aided by the late-week rally in core government bonds.
